content: This is an updated review of the original Cochrane analysis published in 2013. Evidence supports that combining two different analgesics in fixed doses within a single tablet can provide superior pain relief for acute pain and headaches compared to using either drug alone. The effects of the individual drugs in such combinations are generally additive. This principle has been observed in postoperative pain and migraine headache management across various drug combinations and trials. Some ibuprofen-codeine combinations are available over-the-counter (OTC) at lower codeine doses, while higher-dose combinations require a prescription. However, concerns have been raised about the misuse of OTC codeine-containing analgesics. The objective of this review was to evaluate the analgesic efficacy and adverse effects of a single oral dose of ibuprofen combined with codeine for managing acute moderate-to-severe postoperative pain. The methods used allowed for direct comparisons with other analgesics tested in standardized trials with similar methodologies and outcomes. The search for relevant studies included databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Oxford Pain Relief Database, ClinicalTrials.gov, and reference lists of articles. The most recent search was conducted on December 1, 2014. The inclusion criteria were randomized, double-blind, placeboor active-controlled clinical trials investigating single-dose oral ibuprofen plus codeine for acute postoperative pain in adults. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. Pain relief was measured using the area under the pain relief versus time curve, focusing on the proportion of participants achieving at least 50% pain relief over six hours. Risk ratios (RR) and numbers needed to treat to benefit (NNT) were calculated. Data on rescue medication use, median time to rescue medication, and adverse effects were also collected. Analyses were planned for different doses of ibuprofen and codeine, with codeine doses categorized as low (<10 mg), medium (10–20 mg), and high (>20 mg). No new studies were identified since the last review. Data were available from six studies involving 1,342 participants, using various doses of ibuprofen and codeine. Four studies (443 participants) evaluated ibuprofen 400 mg combined with high-dose codeine (25.6 mg to 60 mg). In this group, 64% of participants achieved at least 50% maximum pain relief, compared to 18% in the placebo group. The NNT was 2.2 (95% confidence interval: 1.8 to 2.6), indicating high-quality evidence. Three studies (204 participants) compared ibuprofen plus codeine (any dose) to the same dose of ibuprofen alone. The combination provided better pain relief (69% versus 55%), but the result was only marginally significant, with a relative benefit of 1.3 (95% confidence interval: 1.01 to 1.6), representing moderate-quality evidence. Two studies (159 participants) compared ibuprofen plus codeine to codeine alone. The combination appeared more effective (69% versus 33%), but no formal analysis was conducted. Adverse event rates were similar between the ibuprofen-codeine combination and placebo in these acute studies, based on moderate-quality evidence. In conclusion, the combination of ibuprofen 400 mg and codeine 25.6 mg to 60 mg provides effective pain relief for acute postoperative pain. Limited data suggest that the combination is more effective than either drug alone, with a comparable incidence of adverse events to placebo.
